extracted.intended_audience: educated public; teachers, naturalists, agriculturalists, and educational policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative statements about aesthetic judgement in animals, the effects and practical application of electricity in agriculture, and recommended principles and policy for teaching zoology (especially entomology and vertebrate zoology) in schools and universities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beauty as indicator of health and fitness
rubrics_metrics.description: Our idea of beauty demands that the figure should neither be too fat nor too thin, but should possess that graceful development of all the muscles which is the outward symbol of ability to move and act with ease and effect; we do not admire white cheeks, which are the external mark of weakness or anemia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Preference for features (rosy cheeks, rounded faces, strong and graceful limbs, well-developed chest) is rooted in hereditary selection: tastes that favor traits associated with vigor and reproductive success will be perpetuated. The mere presentation of a typical healthy combination will instinctively rouse the hereditary feeling of beauty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract/formal elements contributing to perceived beauty
rubrics_metrics.description: Even without species-specific hereditary feelings, the strength of purely abstract elements — color, brilliancy, symmetry, form, and minute workmanship — can make an object be pronounced beautiful after its kind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: peacock and humming-bird display such strong color, symmetry and workmanship that humans recognize them as beautiful despite different species-specific tastes. These are the formal aesthetic dimensions to consider when evaluating beauty in animals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sexual selection explains focused aesthetic arousal
rubrics_metrics.description: This feeling will probably be most strongly aroused in each species by the sight of the sex which in that species has undergone the greatest differentiation through sexual selection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implication: the sex exhibiting the most ornamentation (e.g., human females in mankind; certain birds in avian species) will most strongly trigger aesthetic responses among conspecifics; sexual selection is the mechanism generating those traits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between passive selection and active artistic creation
rubrics_metrics.description: Man possesses the active power of direct artistic creation; the birds only possess the passive power of selection from among the forms produced for them by Nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While humans can intentionally create and depict beauty (e.g., on canvas), other animals typically exercise choice among naturally produced variants. Thus birds may produce ornamental harmonies they themselves do not 'understand' fully; some effects (symmetry, feather growth modes) may be incidental rather than consciously admired by the animal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Birds' ranking on an aesthetic scale
rubrics_metrics.description: The actual appearance of birds entitles them to rank, on the whole, higher in the aesthetic scale than any other animals except man.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criteria include graceful shapes (swan, heron), plumes (ostrich, bird-of-paradise), color (sunbird, lory), ornamental crests and lappets (humming-birds, pigeons, parrots), and song (linnet, mocking-bird, nightingale). Causes include free life, rapid motion, developed senses, relative freedom from enemies, and intense intraspecific mate rivalry.

rubrics_metrics.name: Atmospheric electricity influences plant nutrition and growth
rubrics_metrics.description: A plant withdrawn from the influence of atmospheric electricity is subject to marked retardation in its development, so that the quantity of living substance in insulated vegetation is from thirty to fifty per cent less than the production in free air.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chemical analyses showed defective nutrition in plants placed under a metallic cage (faradic cage). Grandeau and Mascart's experiments support that atmospheric electricity affects chlorophyllic protoplasm transformation into glucose, flowering, and fruit-bearing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental insulation method as diagnostic of electrical effects
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiments consisted in placing plants under similar conditions of soil, light, and water, but covering one plant with a cage of iron-wire netting (wires one fiftieth of an inch diameter, mesh six inches by four) acting as a faradic cage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Observed differences (example: tobacco-plant without cage 1.05 m height, 14 leaves, 107 g fresh leaves; under cage 0.69 m, 10 leaves, 70 g) illustrate insulation reduces growth and nutrition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Electricity's role in soil nitrification mediated by plants
rubrics_metrics.description: Electricity does not appear to favor the direct combination of the nitrogen of the air with oxygen, nor with the hydrocarbons of the soil; but it exercises a remarkable influence on the nitrification of the nitrogenized matters of the soil by the intervention of the plant as an electrical conductor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Atmospheric electricity is therefore a preponderating factor in vegetable production; experimental work examined relations between electrical effect and soil nitrification and atmospheric ammonia assimilation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical application to hasten vegetation using electrical surcharge
rubrics_metrics.description: The growth of vegetation may be enhanced twenty-five to fifty per cent by the judicious application of electricity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical arrangement: on an insulated slab place an iron structure with depending points discharging into the atmosphere from an induction machine (estimated potential ~4000–5000 V) maintained day and night for months; alternative low-cost method: metallic points on an insulated framework above plants or wires carried by gas-filled balloons to collect atmospheric electricity and slowly discharge to earth, saturating local atmosphere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Education should emphasize observation and inductive reasoning over rote memorization
rubrics_metrics.description: It is the office of education to direct the mental growth of the individual; and this should be by a developing and not by a cramming process. There is too much burdening of the verbal memory, and too little of the objective memory resulting from the exercise of the mind upon actual objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: What is wanted is more observation, more inductive reasoning, judgment, understanding — in short, intelligent thinking. Natural science should be taught as a constant study of concrete objects, with time devoted on two or more days of each week throughout the student's whole career.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use students' specimens and learn alongside them
rubrics_metrics.description: Teachers should utilize what they can obtain by the help of students. This is dangerous for the unfitted instructor, because he will be constantly approached with new specimens and with questions he cannot answer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Better to have reference books at hand and look things up, or have the student do it, than to miss the instructional opportunity. Instructors may form classes to learn with students when initially unversed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zoology (vertebrate and entomological) is essential in public schools
rubrics_metrics.description: All educational institutions, and public schools especially, should be required to teach vertebrate and entomological zoology in a thorough manner, while the general characteristics of the other branches and a few of their more common and curious representatives should be briefly studied in addition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical entomology is best taught to agricultural-minded youth when deprived of unessential technicalities. It should be prioritized even at the expense of other standard studies because of direct practical value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislative and cooperative measures for insect and bird protection/control
rubrics_metrics.description: We need legislation to enforce — 1. The teaching of entomology and vertebrate zoology. 2. Cooperation in destroying insect-pests. 3. The protection of beneficial insects. 4. The protection of useful birds and their eggs, whether game-birds or not, throughout the entire year.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Entomological legislation (e.g., German insect-laws) can be beneficial; laws, even if imperfectly executed, instruct the people as to their duties. Farmers often must be compelled to cooperate for their own interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical, applied zoology curricula and resources at universities
rubrics_metrics.description: At Cornell University there are special courses pertaining to vertebrates and insects; anatomical department work on the cat as a standard, entomological department attention to injurious or beneficial insects, and complete collections illustrating insects and their habits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Instruction includes use of antidotes and devices against pests; students may elect advanced courses: (1) economic entomology; (2) systematic classification work; (3) comparative anatomy and histology of insects; (4) comparative embryology and metamorphoses. Studies should be conducted with reference to cultivation of crops, breeding and medical treatment of domestic animals, human physiology and hygiene, and doctrines of evolution.
